text.body:
JOURNAL OF SEMITIC STUDIES
ISSN 0021-4480
VOLUME 25 NUMBER 2 AUTUMN 1980
PAUSAL FORMS IN BIBLICAL HEBREW: THEIR FUNCTION, ORIGIN AND SIGNIFICANCE*
E. J. REVELL
UNIVERSITY OF TORONTO
1. INTRODUCTION
Pausal forms are generally (probably universally) held to be conditioned by phonological features similar to the intonation patterns which mark the ends of sentences in English. If this is so, they ought to occur regularly, according to predictable patterns. Their distribution is usually described in terms of the accent system. It is true that as a general rule pausal forms occur with silluq, atnaḥ, and ‘oleb we-yored. In fact a considerable proportion of pausal forms (over 25% in some books) occurs with other accents (even conjunctive accents), and there is a small but significant number of cases in which pausal forms are not used with major pausal accents. The accent system cannot, then, either be the conditioning factor, or reflect it.
2. THE FUNCTION OF PAUSAL FORMS IN PROSE TEXTS
2.1. The Book of Deuteronomy provides excellent illustrations of the positions in which pausal forms occur in biblical prose. About 465 pausal forms occur in this book. Less than 76% of these occur with atnaḥ or silluq. The remaining 24% of the pausal * The original form of this paper was read before the International Organization for Masoretic Studies at the VIIth World Congress of Jewish Studies in Jerusalem, August 1977. Note also that the same vowel and accent signs are used in the Aramaic of the Bible as in the Hebrew, but pausal forms occur in only a few of the cases where they would in Hebrew. Pause is a feature of the language, not a product of the biblical chant.

PAUSAL FORMS IN BIBLICAL HEBREW
forms mostly occur with segolta, zaqef, or tifha; however, 9 occur with revia, 5 with pashta, 3 with telisha, and one with each of zarqa, tevir, geresh, and the conjunctive munah. Thus 21 pausal forms, or nearly 5%, occur with accents of distinctly minor pausal value.
2.2. About 75% of the pausal forms occur at the ends of clauses. Those which occur within clauses can be grouped in two basic categories: those marking the ends of equivalent units used in parallel function, and those which simply divide a clause into two parts. Equivalent units in parallel function can range from a long series of nouns in a list, to two or three prepositional phrases. In such cases a pausal form is not used after every item unless the items are unusually long or significant. As far as can be determined, the usual practice is to group the items in twos or threes, and use a pausal form at the end of each group. Examples are: for a list, Deut. v. 14 (cf. vii. 13 etc.)
לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה כָל מְלָאכָה אַתָּה וּבִנְךָ וּבִתֶּךָ וְעַבְדְּךָ וַאֲמָתֶךָ
... וְשׁוֹרְךָ וַחֲמֹרְךָ וְכָל בְּהֶמְתֶּךָ
and for parallel phrases Deut. xxviii. 67 (cf. xxii. 9, xxxiii. 13 etc.) בַּבֹּקֶר תֹּאמַר ... וּבָעֶרֶב תֹּאמַר ... מִפַּחַד לְבָבְךָ אֲשֶׁר תִּפְחָד
וּמִמַּרְאֵה עֵינֶיךָ אֲשֶׁר תִּרְאֶה׃
It is noteworthy that the items in lists are often grouped in a similar way by the accents, as in Deut. viii. 8 and also by verse divisions, as in Neh. xii. 1 ff. (separating items in a list) or in Deut. ix. 1 f. (separating parallel phrases).
2.3. Where pausal forms are used between phrases which are not syntactically equivalent, they seem generally to occur at the end of the most significant part or "core" of the clause, and to divide it from less important phrases, often explanatory modifiers, which follow.The purpose would seem to be to emphasise the basic statement in the core of the clause. Examples are: Deut. xiii. 18
וְרִחַמְךָ וְהִרְבֶּךָ כַּאֲשֶׁר נִשְׁבַּע לַאֲבֹתֶיךָ׃
where the pausal form is followed by an explanatory modifier (cf. xxv. 13, xxviii. 27 etc.), and Deut. v. 27
קְרַב אַתָּה וּשְׁמָע אֵת כָּל אֲשֶׁר יֹאמַר יהוה אֱלֹהֵינוּ Cf. the similar phenomena in the accentuation called "Supplemental clause" and "Zusatz" in W. Wickes, A treatise on the accentuation of the twenty-one ... books, Oxford 1887, 32, 45, 47, 48, 57, cf. 3 on pp. 53-4.
PAUSAL FORMS IN BIBLICAL HEBREW
where the pausal form separates a verb from its object to empha- sise the command (cf. also Deut. viii. 16, etc.). Again the same sort of division is frequently marked by the accents, or by verse divisions, as in Deut. iv. 47–8 (cf. iv. 41–2, etc.).
2.4. Pausal forms are not generally used at the ends of clauses introducing speech.Thus forms from the root 'mr in Gen. xxxiv. 31 and Deut. xxi. 7 both show contextual forms with atnab. Pausal forms do, however, occur in this position, as in Deut. viii. 17, xviii. 21 (but cf. vii. 17); and xviii. 17 (but cf. i. 42 etc.). The accentuation likewise rarely marks a major pause after an introduction to speech (see Wickes, Twenty-one books, pp. 35 f.), although this may occur (e.g. Gen. xxiii. 5, 10, 14, also 8, but cf. 13). Similarly pausal forms are not generally used before relative clauses introduced by ’šr. There are about 110 other cases in Deuteronomy in which a clause ends in a contextual form. Such clauses are usually closely related to the following clause, and they are usually short, often only a verb form, as in Deut. xiii. 18, v. 27 quoted above (2.3). Deut. xiv. 25 provides a longer example (with no pause at bydk), and Deut. iv. 19 an exceptionally long one ופן תשא ... השׁמימה וראית ... השׁמים ונדחת והשׁתחוית ... ועבדתם It is in this area, where two or more clauses are joined into one unit, that the semantic element governing the use of pausal forms is most apparent. The perception of a semantic relation- ship of this sort is, of course, a matter of individual interpreta- tion. However, there is never serious difficulty in accepting clauses joined this way as a semantic unit, even though it might, in some cases, seem more natural to separate them.E.g. in Deut. ii. 28 it would seem natural to treat the clause-groups ending “I will eat” and “I will drink” as contrasting, and separate them, but there is no pause at w’klty, showing that they were considered as different aspects of the same idea, and so treated as a unit (cf. Deut. ix. 9, 18).
2.5. Pausal forms are used in the same ways in the other prose materials of the Hebrew Bible.In Psalms, Proverbs and Job, the use of pausal forms appears to be determined by poetic structure. The stylistic/semantic unit, the stich, usually ends with a pausal form where these are distinguished (see 7.3 below). In the poetical passages in the Twenty-one books (e.g. in the Latter Prophets) this does not seem to be the general rule, and the use of the pausal forms seems to be governed by principles close to those visible in the prose passages. The details of their use differ, of course, from book to book, but all show the same general pattern. Pausal forms mark the ends of clauses, or of “sentences”, i.e. semantic units formed of two or more clauses. Rarely they occur within clauses, again marking a division made on a 167 II-2
PAUSAL FORMS IN BIBLICAL HEBREW
semantic basis. The proportion of cases in which the presence or absence of a pausal form occasions surprise is too small (no more than 2% or 3%) to disrupt the general regularity of this pattern. In other words the pausal forms act as punctuation, reflecting a logical system of text division.Consistency in stressing an idea is shown by the pausal punctuation in Lev. viii. 15, 19 and 23 (wyšḥṭ), and in 1 Sam. viii. 11, 13, 14, 16 (yqḥ). It must be remembered, however, that both the pausal and accentual punctuation reflect an understanding of the whole context, so that the same or similar wording is not always treated in the same way.
2.6. As the above examples show, this system of division appears to follow the same principles as that represented by the accents, and the two systems very often coincide. Thus words with silluq and (outside the poetical books) atnaḥ almost always show pausal vowelling (if they distinguish it). However, if it is agreed that the pausal forms reflect a logical system of text division, it is necessary to conclude either that the accents reflect a different way of grouping the words of the text into semantic units, or that they do not have this function at all. The pausal forms show clearly that the list in Deut. v. 14 (see 2.2 above) was read in groups of two or three items. In some cases the accent system agrees with the pausal forms in dividing the text in this way, as in Lev. xiv. 54–6.
זאת הַתּוֹרָה לְכָל נֶגַע הַצָּרַעַת וְלַנָּתֶק׃
וּלְצָרַעַת הַבֶּגֶד וּלַבָּיִת׃
וְלַשְׂאֵת וְלַסַּפַּחַת וְלַבֶּהָרֶת׃
The fact that no such agreement between pausal forms and verse division occurs in Deut. v. 14 must mean that if the accents reflect a way of reading the text, that way was, in this verse, different from that reflected by the pausal forms. Similarly the information on the use of pausal forms in Ezekiel xvi, xvii, and xviii given below (see 7.5) must show either that the pausal forms and the accents reflect different ways of grouping the words of the text into semantic units, or that the accent system does not reflect such a grouping.On this function of the accents, see note 1, p. 169. Because the accents represent musical phenomena, not pauses, it is difficult to make a definite statement about their pausal value. In other forms of chant, however, particular musical motifs regularly represent the end of semantic units, and this is generally understood to be the case in the Biblical chant. (See such analyses as those of Levin in JBL LXXXVII (1968), 64–7, Freedman and Cohen in Masoretic Studies 1, 35.) It is commonly said that the pausal value of the biblical accents There is no reason to accept the latter
PAUSAL FORMS IN BIBLICAL HEBREW
alternative.¹ Consequently, it is concluded here that the pausal forms in biblical prose reflect a system of text division which is independent of, and somewhat different from, that reflected by the accents.
2.7. The Masoretic text, then, contains evidence of two different systems of text division, one based on the verse divisions, and marked by the accent signs, and the other marked by the pausal forms through the vowel signs and stress position.² It seems probable that the accent system, which is still the basis for the public recitation of the text, superseded the pausal system, which was at that time already fixed in the traditional pronunciation.³ There is, however, no evidence to show conclusively that one system is earlier than the other. The system of accent signs perfected by the Tiberian masoretes was certainly based on a long tradition,⁴ but it is clear that the pausal system of punctuation also has ancient roots.
depends on the context in which they are used, but if this is the case, i.e. if zaqef (for instance) may or may not mark the end of a semantic unit, then the accentuation cannot have a semantic basis, but only a musical one. In my opinion the correct statement is not that the pausal value of the accents is variable, but that the division of the text which seemed logical when the present accent system was established in it, no longer always seems logical to us today. (Cf., for instance, Jud. vi. 24, where the accentuation makes yhwh the subject of wyqr, against all the commentators.) The value of the accentuation as marking text divisions is noted in the tenth century Hidāyat al-qāri (see Ginsberg, The Massorah III, p. 50, col. 1). Indeed, the Talmudic phrase pisuq tecamim may well reflect recognition of this function (see E. Werner, The sacred bridge, New York 1959, 111). There is other evidence that vowel patterns are independent of accentuation (though usually consistent with it), e.g. the exceptions to the standard rule that (in certain words) segol or (short) qameṣ occurs before maqqef, but ṣere or ḥolem with an accent. Cf. bn in Gen. xxx. 19 and Lev. xxiv. 10; rb in Isa. i. 11, kl in Ps. xxxv. 10 etc. The value of the accents as marking text divisions has long been recognised (note 1), but the function of the pausal forms (i.e. of those which occur with accents other than atnaḥ and silluq) has never been clearly described. Verse division is generally stable in Jewish MSS of all traditions (but the Samaritan accentuation does not always agree). Major differences from BHS in divisions within the verse are rare in Tiberian or Palestinian MSS, more common in Babylonian. There is evidence to suggest that the Tiberian tradition of text division in the Torah may go back to the second century B.C. (Revell, BJRL LIV (1971), 219).

3. THE ORIGIN OF PAUSAL FORMS: EVIDENCE FROM PHONOLOGY
It is generally agreed that pausal forms reflect the vowel patterns of a stage of the Hebrew Language somewhat earlier than that represented by the received vocalisation. That is, they aroseat some period prior to that of the masoretes.If the reconstruction in J. Blau, A grammar of biblical Hebrew (Wiesbaden, 1976), §9.1 is followed, this would have occurred in the fourth stress period, while the Tiberian vocalisation represents the fifth. It is also true, although this has not been noted, that the conditions which created the difference between pausal and contextual forms had ceased to operate by the time the received vocalisation was established. In various forms showing pataḥ or segol in the stress syllable qameṣ appears in pausal position where the orginal vowel was a but, where it was i, the pataḥ or segol is usually retained in pause.This may be seen in forms such as bat, gat, qāmal, zāqanti (Isa. xxxiii. 9, Gen. xviii. 13 etc.), dibbartī, šibbartī, hiṣṣaltā, leqaḥ, neder, etc. Qameṣ reflecting original i occurs only sporadically in such forms. If the two vowels had been the same when the pausal forms were developed, they would have changed in the same way. The fact that pataḥ or segol deriving from original i is not usually replaced by qameṣ in pause, shows that the creation of new pausal forms had ceased before the time when the reflex of original i in these forms became identical to that of original a, that is, before the period represented by any of the three vocalisation systems.The reflex of original i where MT has pataḥ was still different from that of a at the time of Origen, see E. Brønno, Studien über hebräische Morphologie und Vokalismus, Leipzig 1943, 448. A similar conclusion can be drawn from the fact that the few contextual forms which occur with atnaḥ and silluq, and the few pausal forms which occur with conjunctive accents (no doubt also the larger number which occur with minor disjunctives) also remain unchanged.The variants in C. D. Ginsburg's The Old Testament...with the various readings, London 1926, quite often show qameṣ where BHS has pataḥ with atnaḥ in the poetical books, but this affects only these two vowels, not other types of contextual and pausal forms, and so it probably represents hyper- correction based on the rule of thumb that qameṣ was normal with atnaḥ and silluq, pataḥ with other accents. It is clear, then, that the pausal forms were already fixed in the reading tradition when its received form was established by the masoretes. Consequently, their position in the text, and so the system of text division which they represent, must date from some earlier period.
PAUSAL FORMS IN BIBLICAL HEBREW
4. THE ORIGIN OF PAUSAL FORMS: EVIDENCE FROM BIBLICAL LITERATURE
4.1. The majority of pausal forms occur at the ends of clauses, where a stop might be expected in any linguistic tradition. The cases where pausal forms are used within clauses frequently do not coincide with the conventions of other languages, so that if another tradition does use stops in a similar way, the two are likely to be related. Two cases are particularly striking. (1) A pausal form is not usually used at the end of an introduction to speech, which conflicts with the Greek and Latin convention.For the use of pausal forms and accents in the Hebrew text in this situation see p. 167 note 1. A stop is usually marked after an introduction to speech in Byzantine chant (see Studies in Eastern Chant I (1966), 41). That the same was true in earlier times can readily be seen from the Vulgate (the new Benedictine edition, Rome 1966–, attempts to present Jerome's original cola et commata) and from punctuated Greek MSS such as Alexandrinus. (2) Lists are usually divided into groups of two or three items. This contrasts with the accentuation of the Mishna, where a pause is usually marked after every item in a list, agreeing (whether through coincidence or influence) with the Greek convention.For the situation in Mishna MSS see I. Yeivin in Lešonenu XXIV (1959–60), 209, also my forthcoming article in Studies in Eastern Chant IV, para. 1.b(i) of the section "Accentuation of Rabbinic texts", and examples 1:3, 3:2, 4:2, 6. In Codex Alexandrinus items in a list are frequently separated by a space (with a dot in it) as in Exod. i. 2–4, Lev. xiv. 54–6. This is presumably the usage described by Hermogenes Rhetor as "to kat' onoma kommatikon" (Opera, ed. H. Rabe = Rhetores graeci VI, Leipzig 1913, 316).
4.2. In many cases the pausal forms within a clause appear to be used for emphasis. They either draw attention to what precedes, before some modifier is added, or they separate the parts of a syntactic unit (such as the verb and its object) and so cause suspense, and emphasise what follows (see 2.3). Interjections may perform a similar function. The phrase n’m yhwh is usually used at the end of a clause, but quite often occurs as an interjection within a clause. In these cases it often occurs in positions similar to those in which pausal forms are used within clauses, and may plausibly be interpreted as having a similar function.
4.3. The situation in which n’m yhwh appears within clauses can be grouped as follows:
4.3.1. n’m yhwh may be used after an "adverbial introduction"
PAUSAL FORMS IN BIBLICAL HEBREW
but before the “core” of the clause in which the main idea is expressed. The adverbial introduction consists of one or two prepositional phrases, or of an adverb (often ‘th), and is usually concerned with time, as in 1 Sam. ii. 30, Isa. xxii. 25, Jer. v. 18, viii. 1, xxi. 7, xxxi. 1, l. 4, 20, Joel ii. 12, Mic. iv. 6, Hag. ii. 23, Zech. iii. 10, xii. 4. The adverbial introduction may also be concerned with space, as in Ezek. xx. 40, or with manner, as in Jer. l. 40.
כמהפכת אלהים את סדם . . . נאם יהוה לא ישב שם איש׃
In a similar way n’m yhwh is used after lkn introducing a consequence in 1 Sam. ii. 30 and in Isa. i. 24. Group I is the most common situation in which n’m yhwh is used within clauses. Parallels in the use of pausal forms are not common.See, however, Num. xi. 9 and Esth. i. 10 for the use of pausal forms after an introductory phrase referring to time, and Num. xxxv. 8 for the use of one after a phrase expressing manner:
איש כפי נחלתו אשר ינחלו יתן מעריו ללוים׃ One can also compare the use of pausal forms after invocations in 1 Kings xvii. 20, 21, complex subjects in Num. xviii. 1, 1, xix. 16, and “casus pendens” in Num. xxx. 14, 1 Kings v. 19, etc.
4.3.2. n’m yhwh used after the “core” of the clause, which expresses the main idea, but before some “explanatory modifiers”.Such explanatory modifiers may modify the verb of the clause, as in Jer. xiii. 11, xvii. 24, xxv. 7, Ezek. xxxvi. 23, cf. the pausal form in Num. xxii. 18. The phrase may similarly modify the “headword” of the predicate of a non-verbal clause, as the infinitive phrase in Jer. i. 19
כי אתך אני נאם יהוה להצילך׃
(So also Jer. xxx. 11, xlix. 5, Ezek. xliii. 19.) Cf. the pausal form in 2 Sam. iii. 12
והנה ידי עמך להסב אליך את כל ישראל׃ Phrases following n’m yhwh may also modify other parts of the preceding core of the clause. In this case they typically expand an It is also, of course, true that ‘th does not appear in pausal form in parallel cases where n’m yhwh is not used, although it often does have a relatively strong pausal accent, as in Gen. iv. 11, xii. 19, xx.7. This use of n’m yhwh does, however, correspond to usage typical of the accent system, see Wickes, Twenty-one books, p. 47. The accents often divide clauses in a similar way, see p. 166, note 1.

idea given in the core of the clause.In Jer. l. 35 and Zeph. iii. 8 this occurs in a prepositional phrase, cf. the pausal form in Isa. xiv. 15 or Deut. xxx. 9. In Jer. xv. 3 a noun phrase is expanded in this way.
... ופקדתי עליהם ארבע משפחות נאם יהוה את החרב להרג ואת
(so also Jer. xvi. 5, xxix. 11), cf. the pausal form in 1 Kings iii. 13
וגם אשר לא שאלת נתתי לָךְ גם עשר גם כבוד
The element expanded may even be the pronominal morph in the verb form, as in Amos iii. 10 (cf. the pausal form in Lev. xxv. 41), and similar usage occurs in non-verbal clauses, as Isa. xxx. 1, Jer. xxi. 13, xxiii. 30, 31, li. 25, Ezek. xvi. 30 (cf. the pausal form in 2 Sam. xii. 1). In some cases the phrases following nʾm yhwh express an addition to some item in the core of the clause rather than an expansion of it; that is, nʾm yhwh stands between equivalent units in parallel syntactic function (see 2.2 above). This occurs in a verbal clause in Jer. xix. 12
כן אעשה למקום הזה נאם יהוה וליושביו
Cf. the pausal form in Deut. xxviii. 67 quoted in 2.2 above. There is a similar situation in a non-verbal clause in Isa. xliii. 10 (cf. the pausal form in Gen. xxix. 19).
4.3.3. nʾm yhwh may occur within the “core” of the clause; that is, in cases where the basic idea of the clause is not intelligible (as it is in 4.3.1 and 4.3.2) without the phrases which either precede or follow nʾm yhwh. For instance, nʾm yhwh occurs between the verb and its object in Jer. xlviii. 35
והשבתי למואב נאם יהוה מעלה במה ומקטיר לאלהיו׃
Also Jer. xlviii. 30, and compare the pausal form in Deut. v. 27 (2.3 above), also Isa. lxiv. 3. It occurs in various other positions within verbal clauses in Jer. xxxiv. 17, Zeph. i. 10, Zech. ii. 9. Similarly it occurs before the object of a participle in a non-verbal clause in Amos vi. 14
כי הנני מקים עליכם בית ישראל נאם יהוה אלהי הצבאות גוי
This isolation of a single word at the end of a clause has a striking The accents divide clauses in a similar way in Gen. xxiv. 24, and in several examples listed by Wickes, Twenty-one books, on p. 40 under vi.

The adverbial introduction consists of one or two prepositional phrases, or of an adverb (often ‘th), and is usually concerned with time, as in 1 Sam. ii. 30, Isa. xxii. 25, Jer. v. 18, viii. 1, xxi. 7, xxxi. 1, l. 4, 20, Joel ii. 12, Mic. iv. 6, Hag. ii. 23, Zech. iii. 10, xii. 4. The adverbial introduction may also be concerned with space, as in Ezek. xx. 40, or with manner, as in Jer. l. 40.

In some cases the phrases following n’m yhwh express an addition to some item in the core of the clause rather than an expansion of it; that is, n’m yhwh stands between equivalent units in parallel syntactic function (see 2.2 above). This occurs in a verbal clause in Jer. xix. 12
כּן אעשה למקום הזה נאם יהוה וליושביו
Cf. the pausal form in Deut. xxviii. 67 quoted in 2.2 above. There is a similar situation in a non-verbal clause in Isa. xliii. 10 (cf. the pausal form in Gen. xxix. 19).
4.3.3. n’m yhwh may occur within the “core” of the clause; that is, in cases where the basic idea of the clause is not intelligible (as it is in 4.3.1 and 4.3.2) without the phrases which either precede or follow n’m yhwh. For instance, n’m yhwh occurs between the verb and its object in Jer. xlviii. 35
והשבתי למואב נאם יהוה מעלה במה ומקטיר לאלהיו׃
Also Jer. xlviii. 30, and compare the pausal form in Deut. v. 27 (2.3 above), also Isa. lxiv. 3. It occurs in various other positions within verbal clauses in Jer. xxxiv. 17, Zeph. i. 10, Zech. ii. 9. Similarly it occurs before the object of a participle in a non-verbal clause in Amos vi. 14
כי הנני מקים עליכם בית ישראל נאם יהוה אלהי הצבאות גּוֹי
This isolation of a single word at the end of a clause has a striking The accents divide clauses in a similar way in Gen. xxiv. 24, and in several examples listed by Wickes, Twenty-one books, on p. 40 under vi.
PAUSAL FORMS IN BIBLICAL HEBREW
parallel in the use of the pausal form in Jer. xiii. 13 (also Jer. viii. 1).
כה אמר יהוה הנני ממלא את כל ישבי הארץ הזּאת ואת . . .
ואת . . . ואת . . . ואת כל ישבי ירושלם שִׁכָּרוֹן׃
4.4. Clauses are similarly interrupted by other word groups – most obviously 'mr yhwh which appears, at least in some cases, to function as a free variant of n’m yhwh (e.g. Hag. ii. 9, and cf. Jer. xlix. 18 with Jer. l. 40). 'mr yhwh is used after an adverbial introduction (cf. group I of n’m yhwh) in Isa. xlix. 5, and Jer. xlix. 18. It stands before an explanatory modifier in Isa. lix. 21 (cf. group II) and in the same verse it stands after the title to a list
ואני זאת בריתי אותם אמר יהוה רוחי . . . ודברי . . .
Cf. 4.3.2 above, and the pausal form in Deut. xiv. 4
זאת הבהמה אשר תֹּאכֵל֫וּ שור שה כשבים ושה עזים׃
Finally, 'mr yhwh is used between the parts of a non-verbal clause (cf. 4.3.3), in Isa. xlviii. 22 (cf. lvii. 21), as is another interjection, ly 'mr, in Isa. xlv. 24
אך ביהוה לי אמר צדקות וָעֹז
Cf. 4.3.3 above, and the pausal form in Isa. xxiv. 17 (also Jer. xlviii. 43)
פחד ופחת וָפָח עליך יושב הָאָרֶץ׃
(or, in a prose context, Num. iii. 34).
4.5. In groups 4.3.2 and 4.3.3, then, the similarity of the positions in which n’m yhwh and similar interjections are used to those in which the pausal forms are used is very striking. This seems clear evidence that the authors of these passages found it logical to break their clauses in the same positions as did the readers who produced the pausal forms. The interjections are represented in translations, and their positions have become familiar. However, the punctuation of translations (ancient or modern) offers no support for the idea that the parallel uses of the pausal forms represent any natural or universal logic. It is, therefore, reasonable to suggest an organic connection between 174
PAUSAL FORMS IN BIBLICAL HEBREW
the system of punctuation represented by the pausal forms, and the conventions of clause division represented by the interjections in the passages cited.¹
5. THE ORIGIN OF PAUSAL FORMS: EVIDENCE FROM THE STELE OF MESHA
5.1. The use of the punctuation mark in the inscription of Mesha is also of interest here. This mark is usually placed at the end of a clause, marking off single clauses or (more commonly) groups of two or more clauses.² As with the pausal punctuation, a division is not marked after an introduction to speech (ll. 6, 14, 24–5), nor before a relative clause (ll. 28–9), nor usually before explanatory clauses introduced by ky (ll. 3–4, 5, 27), although as in the pausal system, exceptions may occur (l. 17). In three cases the mark is used within a clause, and in two of these it separates items in a list:
ll. 15–17 /w'ḥzh w'hrg kl[h] šb't 'lpn g[b]rn w[gr]n/wgbrt w[gr]t wrḥmt/
ll. 29–30 /w'nk bnty[ ]b' wbt dbltn/wbt b'lm'n...
(Cf. the pausal form in 1 Kings ix. 17, and 2.2 above). In the third case the punctuation mark appears to stand before what has been called above an “explanatory modifier”, but the context is broken and the restoration uncertain: ll. 3–4 /w'ś hbmt z't lkmš bqrhh/bm[t y]š' ky hš'ny... (cf. the pausal form in 1 Kings v. 31, Gen. xxxi. 18, etc.).
5.2. These marks in the Mesha inscription certainly represent a logical system of punctuation, although some anomalies

suggest that there may be errors in their use.The main problem is in lines 7–8 where the two clauses /wyśr'l ’bd ’bd ‘lm wyrš ‘mry ’t ’[r]ṣ mhdb’ are marked as a single unit, whereas the content appears to require a major break between them. The passage could be understood “(He threatened this in my days, but I triumphed over him and his dynasty.) And Israel suffered a permanent setback, despite Omri’s seizure of MHDB’. (Israel occupied it for forty years, but KMŠ restored it in my day.)” It is questionable whether the translation of wyrš as “although he had taken possession of” can be justified, but a translation which ignores the punctuation without comment (as all that I know do) is equally unsatisfactory. A lesser problem is the fact that in two of the cases where a stop is marked within a clause, none is marked at its end, but cf. the biblical verse division in cases like Lev. xiv. 57, Neh. xii. 7. The significance of a Moabite inscription for Biblical Hebrew may also be questioned. However, the language and thought-world represented seem close enough to those of the Book of Kings to warrant the use of the inscription in the present context. Consequently, it seems justifiable to claim that the punctuation of this inscription provides some support for the idea that the pausal forms of the Hebrew Bible reflect patterns of formation of speech units characteristic of the language of the Biblical period.
6. THE FUNCTION AND ORIGIN OF PAUSAL FORMS: CONCLUSIONS
6.1. Pausal forms in the received text appear (with rare exceptions) in positions easily acceptable as the ends of sense units, that is, at a division in the text which is either logical, or serves some special purpose, such as emphasis. The units so terminated consist of a clause, or a group of clauses or (less commonly), part of a clause. The system of text division represented by these pausal forms, that is the system of grouping phrases and clauses into sense units, appears to follow conventions similar (in some cases) to those which can be seen in the language of the prophets (as it has come down to us), and possibly even in the punctuation of the Mesha incription. It is scarcely probable that this similarity in the logic behind the division of texts shown in these different sources reflects any academic theory of punctuation, as arose from the Greek schools of rhetoric and textual criticism. It seems virtually certain that in all these cases the basis of the text division was the natural patterns of the language, the division of speech into sense units delimited by intonation patterns. Such intonation patterns, an integral part of the sound system
PAUSAL FORMS IN BIBLICAL HEBREW
of the language, would naturally have been used in the oratory of the prophets, or in the reading of texts. These intonation patterns evidently became a fixed part of the biblical reading tradition, and so affected its vowel patterns, producing the pausal forms.
6.2. After this fixation had occurred the pausal forms died out of living usage, so that new pausal forms were not created where suitable vowel patterns came into being, or where a different division of the text left a contextual form at the end of a unit. The intonation patterns which gave rise to the pausal forms were evidently transmuted into, or replaced by, the musical patterns of the chant, which thus took over the function of defining the boundaries of (and divisions within) semantic units. As a result the distinction between pausal and contextual vowelling lost its function, becoming simply one of a number of types of such functionless variations preserved in the reading tradition. The masoretic lists of cases where qameṣ occurs with zaqef, or pataḥ with atnaḥ or silluq, show that the relation between the pausal forms and the accents was recognised, but the incompleteness of these lists suggests that the recognition was late. Whether this is so or not, the masoretic tradition did preserve the pausal forms faithfully even in these apparently anomalous cases, and the fact that the patterns which gave rise to them can still be recognised constitutes an important testimony to the antiquity and reliability of the masoretic tradition.
7. IMPLICATIONS FOR THE STUDY OF BIBLICAL LITERATURE
7.1. The assumption that the pausal forms of the Bible (or some of them) reflect a method of reading customary at some time before that of the Masoretes has no doubt been made by many others,Cf. the suggestion in G. Bergsträsser, Hebräische Grammatik, Leipzig 1918, I, 29u. and certainly the phenomenon of pause in Arabic would support it. It is, however, of value to have such assumptions confirmed by a detailed investigation, and this investigation has the merit of revealing the high probability of direct connection between the method of reading reflected by the pausal forms and the patterns of speech or oratory of the biblical period. This does not, of course, imply that the method of reading
PAUSAL FORMS IN BIBLICAL HEBREW
reflected by the pausal forms persisted unchanged from ancient times,That is, the logic behind the division remained the same, but the places where individual divisions were marked may have changed, as occurred when the division marked by the accents superseded that marked by the pausal forms. but it does mean that it reflects ancient patterns of logic and expression.
7.2. The significance of the conclusion that the pausal forms reflect an early stage of the reading tradition is not limited to its interest for the history of that tradition. These forms reflect the way in which the text was commonly understood at some period prior to that of the Masoretes, and can therefore provide information significant for the history of the development of literary units, from the forms identified by scholarly analysis as original, to those of the received text.The examples below owe a great deal to a study by W. D. Arbo on Lamentations and other poetical passages in the Twenty-one books, and one by Sandra Demson on the Book of Ezekiel, made in connection with a graduate seminar at Toronto.
7.3. The vast majority of the verses in the Book of Proverbs are composed of two stichs, each ending (if the word can form one) in a pausal form. In three anomalous cases (compared to 387 with pausal forms), the first stich ends in a contextual form (xxiv. 4, 30, xxx. 21). In longer verses, however, contextual forms occur much more commonly at the end of stichs (xxiii. 5, xxx. 9, 14, 15, 16, 17 compared to 34 with pausal forms). This suggests that these longer verses were also read as composed of two stichs, as suggested by the accents, and not as three or four, as suggested by the wording.The relationship between the verse division and the use of pausal forms is also very striking in the Book of Lamentations. In the Psalms, however, pausal forms not uncommonly reflect the reading of verses as three stichs (e.g. l. 7, lvi. 9, cxvi. 16, cxxxviii. 2).
7.4. Pausal forms in poetical passages in the prophets similarly sometimes reflect a reading of these passages in individual stichs, as suggested by the wording, as in Isa. lxv. 13. However, verses 8, 9, 12, 15 and 19 of this chapter show stichs which do not end in pausal forms. Presumably, then, the pausal forms reflect a reading tradition which recognised a variety of literary forms in this section, not a poem composed throughout in stichs of more or less equal length.
7.5. The allegory in Ezek. xvi. 1–34 is written as narrative prose, with verbs standing predominantly at the beginning of
PAUSAL FORMS IN BIBLICAL HEBREW
their clauses. Pausal forms occur regularly with atnaḥ and silluq (23 cases), but it is common to find other clauses ending with contextual forms (14 cases in 34 verses, 10 with zaqef). In the more direct preaching in Ezek. xvii. 11-xviii. 20, verbs are commonly placed at the ends of clauses. Clauses regularly end with pausal forms, both with atnaḥ, and silluq (11 cases), and with other accents (16 cases in 34 verses, 13 with zaqef). Pausal forms occur twice within a clause. Only four clauses end with contextual forms (one with zaqef). Clearly the use of pausal forms suggests that different styles of reading were used in these two prose sections, corresponding to their differences in literary style and content.
7.6. As long as it is held, as it is now, that the distribution of pausal forms is conditioned by the accent system except for (a small proportion of) inexplicable anomalies, the way in which these forms are used in the passages described above can be of no interest. It is the author's hope that this article has demonstrated that the distribution of pausal forms is, in fact, due to the generally accurate preservation of an ancient tradition. If so, the questions raised by the ways in which these forms occur in literary units like those described above are of considerable interest and importance to the history of biblical literature.
